scenarios.title: Repair an application’s file layout
scenarios.summary: Use file purpose to repair a stopped application’s configuration, reference data, persistent state and log locations.
scenarios.objective: Beacon is stopped. Work as Alex in the supplied delegated Beacon subfolders; parent hierarchy folders remain protected. Place the host settings, locally installed read-only reference, persistent changing progress and event log into their corresponding Beacon folders under /etc, /usr/local/share, /var/lib and /var/log. Keep each original filename. Finish with exactly the appropriate one file in each of the four Beacon folders; remove the wrong-location copies without losing their text. Keep every /work/intake original’s text and mode, the private note’s text and mode, and /etc/site-policy.txt unchanged. Investigate with the simulated terminal, make the file changes and choose Check work.
scenarios.retry_guidance: If a file is missing or misplaced, cat the named path and the matching /work/intake original. Settings control operation; labels are reference data; cursor.db is durable changing progress, not disposable cache or a log. List the affected Beacon folders with ls -a, repair the role placement and check again. Keep the originals intact.

scenarios.simplifications:
FHS3.0 role practice, not full LPIC104.7 coverage. No locate/updatedb/which/whereis indexes or real installation.

Alex is an ordinary simulated user. Supplied application subdirectories are delegated to Alex while parent hierarchy directories remain root-owned; no sudo or root override.

The application is stopped. Files are bounded UTF-8 teaching fixtures, not live databases, binary data, mounts or service storage.

Only the existing literal terminal subset is supported: no wildcard expansion, pipes, redirection, recursive copy, shell scripting or host execution. find accepts one start, quoted basename patterns, -type f/d and optional leading -maxdepth.

Outcomes check declared file contents, names and requested metadata. They do not prove a particular investigation command was run, assess real system policy, or promise a globally exclusive copy outside the declared handover.

terminal_teaching.prerequisite_note: You have practised paths, cat, single-file cp/mv and quoted find patterns. Type in the simulated terminal and choose Run. Alex has permission only in the supplied app/work folders; do not use sudo.

concepts.title: Choose a directory by the file’s job
concepts.text: A configuration file tells a program what to do. A reference table is input that the program reads without updating. A checkpoint remembers changing work between runs. A log records events. A familiar-looking filename is a clue, not proof: use cat to read the supplied small text files.

concepts.title: Four locations, four purposes
concepts.text: For this site, /etc/APP holds host configuration; /usr/local/share/APP holds locally installed reference data that is not tied to a particular kind of processor; /var/lib/APP holds persistent changing state; /var/log/APP holds event logs. APP means the application’s own folder. This is not a rule that every local program must use /etc: /usr/local/etc is also a valid local configuration location.

concepts.title: Relocate safely
concepts.text: mv SOURCE DESTINATION changes a file’s location; cp leaves the source in place. Here the application is stopped and Alex may change its application folders. Root-owned parent folders remain protected. This is a supplied training arrangement, not permission to rearrange a running service or system folders on a real computer.

concepts.title: Verify the files, not just the command
concepts.text: A silent mv usually means success. List each application folder and inspect its text. Retain the separate intake originals and private note. The reference files are called read-only data because the application does not update them; that description does not mean their permissions can never allow an administrator to replace them.

terminal_teaching.inputs: Lantern is a separate stopped example. Its four application folders contain one misplaced file each; independent originals are in /work/demo-originals. All paths are virtual.
terminal_teaching.try_change: After the worked moves, move /var/lib/lantern/cursor.db back to /usr/local/share/lantern/cursor.db. List both folders: the same text is now in the wrong role. Move it back and inspect the restored location.

scenarios.title: Find an active application’s support files
scenarios.summary: Follow active configuration across the hierarchy and assemble an exact, renamed support handover without changing application files.
scenarios.objective: As Alex, locate Harbor’s active configuration below /etc. Inspect it and locate the reference, checkpoint and event files it names across /usr/local/share, /var/lib and /var/log. Copy the active configuration as /work/support/config.txt, its reference as reference.txt, its checkpoint as checkpoint.txt and its events as activity.txt. These are handover names, not new application source paths. Finish /work/support with exactly those four files, using current active text rather than archived or neighbouring content. Preserve the text and paths of every supplied application/archived/other source and the site-policy/private note; keep private-note.txt at mode 600. Do not copy private notes into the handover. Use supported commands, inspect the result and choose Check work.
scenarios.retry_guidance: If a support file has the wrong text, cat /etc/harbor/site.conf and compare its named active source with the failed output path. A same-name archive or neighbouring file is not current. ls -a /work/support reveals extra hidden copies; missing or moved application sources must also be restored before the handover passes.

terminal_teaching.prerequisite_note: You have practised paths, cat, single-file cp/mv and quoted find patterns. Type in the simulated terminal and choose Run. Alex has permission only in the supplied app/work folders; do not use sudo.

concepts.title: Start with the directory’s purpose
concepts.text: Host configuration belongs in this site’s /etc application folder. Local reference data is under /usr/local/share, persistent progress under /var/lib, and events under /var/log. A support copy in /work is a handover copy; it does not change the application’s own configuration or installation.

concepts.title: Find candidates, then inspect the relationship
concepts.text: find /etc -type f -name 'site.conf' lists matching ordinary files below one starting folder. Quote patterns such as '*.conf'. find matches paths, not file contents: cat the active application’s configuration to learn which reference, checkpoint and event files it actually names. Archived and neighbouring files can have the same filename.

concepts.title: Keep originals and name the handover clearly
concepts.text: cp SOURCE DESTINATION copies one ordinary file without moving its source. The four requested handover names describe their roles. A checkpoint is not an event log; an archived file is not current just because its name matches. Check source paths and text before making each copy.

concepts.title: Inspect after a change
concepts.text: ls -a reveals extra hidden handover files as well as ordinary names. cat checks the copied text. Inspect the finished handover and confirm the originals are still in place. Several command sequences can reach that result.

terminal_teaching.inputs: Orchard is a different application. The example begins in /etc/orchard. Its configuration names three current paths; archive folders contain misleading same-name files. /work/support starts empty.
terminal_teaching.try_change: Replace /work/support/activity.txt with a copy of /var/log/orchard/archive/events.log. cat the output: the filename is correct but its RETIRED marker makes the contents wrong. Recopy the active log named by /etc/orchard/site.conf.
